title: How LLMs Are Trained
brief: Large language models start out guessing the next word, then learn to follow instructions, align with humans, and verify their own reasoning. Let's walk through the modern training stack from pretraining to scaling trade-offs.

questions.question: Why does training a language model to predict the next word teach it real facts and grammar instead of random guessing?
questions.answer: Guessing the next word well across billions of sentences forces the model to learn real patterns. To predict what comes next in science, stories, or code, it must absorb facts, grammar, and logic.
key_points: Predicting the next word well across real text requires learning the underlying facts, grammar, or logic behind it
Training on massive amounts of diverse writing rewards deeper patterns over lucky surface guesses
questions.hint: Think about finishing a mystery novel or a history textbook line without knowing who did what.
questions.fun_fact: In an early OpenAI experiment on product reviews, simply predicting the next character made one single neuron learn to track positive or negative mood.

questions.question: How does supervised fine-tuning change a raw pretrained language model into an assistant you can actually chat with?
questions.answer: A raw base model only tries to continue whatever text you type, like an advanced autocomplete. Supervised fine-tuning trains it on curated prompt and answer pairs written in a helpful style. That teaches the model to follow your instructions instead of just extending your prompt.
key_points: It trains the base model on curated prompt-and-answer examples showing helpful instruction following
This shifts the model away from simple text continuation toward answering user requests
questions.hint: Picture handing a bright student hundreds of ideal dialogue scripts so they copy the back-and-forth format.
questions.fun_fact: In the original InstructGPT study, human raters preferred a fine-tuned 1.3-billion-parameter model over a raw model more than 100 times larger.

questions.question: How does LoRA fine-tune a giant language model on modest hardware without updating all of the original weights?
questions.answer: LoRA freezes all the original model weights so they stay untouched during training. Instead, it attaches tiny low-rank adapter matrices that learn only the needed weight updates. Training just those small adapters slashes memory needs and cuts trainable parameters sharply.
key_points: It trains tiny low-rank adapter matrices attached alongside the frozen original layers
The base model weights stay frozen so far fewer parameters need gradient updates
This cuts training memory needs sharply compared to updating the whole model
questions.hint: Think of placing thin transparent overlays on an encyclopedia rather than reprinting every single page.
questions.fun_fact: Once LoRA training finishes, you can merge the tiny adapter weights straight back into the frozen model so it runs with zero extra delay.

questions.question: How does reinforcement learning from human feedback turn human answer rankings into better responses from a language model?
questions.answer: First, humans compare pairs of model replies and choose the better one. Teams use those preference pairs to train a separate reward model that predicts human choices. Reinforcement learning then pushes the language model to produce replies that earn higher reward scores.
key_points: Human preference rankings train a separate reward model to score which replies people prefer
Reinforcement learning then updates the language model to maximize scores from that reward model
Automating feedback through the reward model lets training run across far more steps than humans could grade live
questions.hint: Picture a chef practicing nonstop for a stand-in food critic who studied past dinner reviews.
questions.fun_fact: OpenAI built the original InstructGPT reward model using preference rankings from a team of only about 40 human contractors.

questions.question: How does Direct Preference Optimization, or DPO, simplify preference training compared to classic RLHF?
questions.answer: DPO removes the separate reward model and the complex reinforcement learning loop completely. Instead, it trains the language model directly on pairs of preferred and rejected replies. The update simply raises the odds of the winning answer and lowers the losing one.
key_points: It removes the need for a separate reward model
It trains the language model directly on preferred and rejected answer pairs
Skipping the extra reinforcement learning loop makes training simpler and steadier
questions.hint: Think about firing the middleman critic and coaching the writer straight from thumbs-up and thumbs-down comparisons.
questions.fun_fact: The DPO paper is subtitled Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model, because its math turns the model's own probabilities into an implicit score.

questions.question: During RLHF, why do engineers add a KL penalty that pulls the model back toward its starting reference version?
questions.answer: Without that tether, the model learns to exploit blind spots in the imperfect reward model. This reward hacking can produce repetitive gibberish or flattering fluff that scores high yet fails users. The KL penalty punishes drifting too far, keeping language natural while still improving replies.
key_points: It stops reward hacking, where the model games flaws in the reward model or drifts into unnatural, repetitive, or unhelpful text
Keeping the model tethered preserves fluent language from the reference model while still raising quality
Any learned reward model is an imperfect stand-in for true human preferences
questions.hint: Imagine a dog chasing treats so eagerly that it runs off the trail when nobody holds the leash.
questions.fun_fact: Human preference training can also trigger sycophancy, where an assistant agrees with a user's wrong belief just to sound pleasing.

questions.question: Why does reinforcement learning with verifiable math or code checks unlock deep reasoning better than human-preference RLHF?
questions.answer: Automated checks test whether a final math answer or code solution actually passes. That objective signal is hard to hack, unlike human judges who can fall for smooth-sounding nonsense. Chasing real correctness teaches the model to think longer, backtrack, and fix its own mistakes.
key_points: Verifiable checks reward objective correctness that is hard to game, unlike subjective human ratings
Pushing for real right answers teaches the model to think longer, backtrack, and fix mistakes
Human judges can fall for smooth-sounding wrong answers, especially in long reasoning traces
questions.hint: Compare an unblinking lock that only opens for the exact key against a teacher swayed by polished prose.
questions.fun_fact: Trained with an algorithm called GRPO, DeepSeek-R1-Zero spontaneously learned to double-check its math, though it sometimes mixed English and Chinese mid-thought.

questions.question: Chinchilla scaling balances model size and data for the lowest training cost, so why do labs now train smaller models on far more tokens?
questions.answer: Chinchilla scaling only minimizes the one-time compute cost of training the model. Once a model launches, serving millions of user queries costs far more over its lifetime. Over-training a smaller model reaches high quality while keeping everyday inference fast and cheap.
key_points: Smaller models are much faster and cheaper to run during inference across millions of user queries
Chinchilla scaling only minimizes one-time training cost and ignores long-term serving costs
Feeding a smaller model far more tokens recovers high accuracy without making it bigger at runtime
questions.hint: Compare the upfront sticker price of buying a car against the gas bill you pay every week for years.
questions.fun_fact: Meta trained its 8-billion-parameter Llama 3 model on 15 trillion tokens, more than 90 times the data the Chinchilla rule suggested.
